library(tidyverse)

## ARIMA vs ets

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
```

```{r}
liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "Beer, Wine, and Liquor Store Sales", x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in Liquor Store Sales", x = NULL, y = "log(sales)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

2.1b steady upward trend the whole time. December is way higher than every other month, Jan and feb are the lowest, summer is a little above average. the December spikes get bigger as sales go up, logs makes sense

```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

2.2a ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)[12] with drift and ETS(A,A,A). the ARIMA only takes a seasonal difference, this month - same month last year, no regular difference. ets is additive error, additive trend, additive seasonality

```{r}
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```

2.2b not white noise. Ljung-Box is about 120 with p ≈ 0 so there's still some structure left

2.3a 216 forecast origins. 336 months - the first 120, - the last one we drop

```{r}
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

2.3b first forecast is jan 2002, last is dec 2019. ARIMA is the most accurate, then ETS, then SNAIVE behind. RMSE and MAE agree

```{r}
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)
```

2.4 ARIMA vs ETS: DM = -2.91, p = 0.004. ARIMA vs SNAIVE: DM = -10.76. ARIMA is much better than both. I'd use ARIMA

## Forecast Combination

```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

3a combo is in between. better than ETS but worse than ARIMA

```{r}
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```

3b the errors are really correlated (0.88) so averaging doesn't cancel much out. and ARIMA was already significantly better than ETS, so mixing in ETS drags it down

## VAR vs. BVAR

4.1c 120 forecasts per variable, from 1990 Q1 to 2019 Q4

4.2 VAR(1) is better for 7 of the 8 variables, only inflation is basically a tie. VAR(4) has way more coefficients to estimate so the extra estimation noise hurts more than the extra lags help

```{r}
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

4.3b BVAR with λ = 0.3 beats the VAR(4) for all 8 variables. same variables and lags, only difference is the prior shrinking the coefficients, which cuts down estimation noise. vs the VAR(1) it's mixed, BVAR wins for investment, inflation and the 10 year yield, VAR(1) wins the rest. with λ = 0.05 it gets worse for most variables, especially employment and inflation, so too much shrinkage. no, the winner's RMSE isn't a fair estimate since we picked it because it did best on this same sample

```{r}
readRDS("results/dm_gdp.rds")
readRDS("results/dm_infl.rds")
```

4.3c GDP: DM = 2.14, p = 0.035, so BVAR is significantly better at 5%. inflation: DM = 1.45, p = 0.149, not significant. so a lot of the differences in the table could just be noise

## Factor Model

```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,
         "2" = d(x),
         "3" = d(d(x)),
         "4" = log(x),
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]
dim(fm)

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```

5.1c INDPRO is a growth rate (code 5). PAYEMS is also a growth rate (5). CPIAUCSL is the change in the growth rate, so the change in inflation (6). FEDFUNDS is just the first difference (2). the fed funds rate is already a percent and can be near zero, so logging it doesn't make sense, you just difference it

```{r}
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))
summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```

5.2a about 29.5%, same as in class

```{r}
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

5.2c factor 1 is mostly employment and industrial production, and it drops in recessions. so it's basically real activity / the business cycle. factor 2 is mostly CPI and PCE prices, so it's an inflation factor

```{r}
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```

5.3 got 0.617 and 0.589, same as class. using full sample factors would be cheating because they'd use future data we wouldn't have at the time of the forecast, so the results would look better than they really are

```{r}
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)
  g <- lv$g
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL") |> knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

5.4 yes, the factors help. RMSE goes from 2.11 to 1.89, about 10.6% lower. p = 0.0004 so it's significant

## Reflection

simple models were hard to beat lots of the time. VAR(1) beat VAR(4), and the combo didn't beat ARIMA. the same thing happened, estimating fewer things or keeping things simple cuts down on noise. shrinkage, equal weights, and factors all do that in different ways. more complex isn't better unless it actually adds info, like the factors did for inflation.
